body:
From the pre-release security review of the server's network interface
(2026-07-26). Post-1.8.1.

## Problem

server/README.md:362 claims:

    `/login` itself does *not* enumerate (it returns the same
    `invalid_credentials` for an unknown email and a wrong password).

The status code and body are identical, but the TIMING is not. auth.py:127 only
calls check_password_hash when the account row was found, so the scrypt work
(werkzeug 3.1.8 default, scrypt:32768:8:1) happens only for real accounts.

Measured, median of 12 requests each:

    existing account, wrong password : 196.54 ms
    unknown account                  :   3.74 ms
    ratio                            : 52x

52x is trivially observable over a network. This is a working account-existence
oracle, and it contradicts a documented security claim — which is worse than an
undocumented gap, because an operator reading the README will not compensate for
it at the proxy.

Related note (not a bug, but the reason the gap is expensive): each login
against a KNOWN account costs ~32 MB of RAM and ~195 ms of CPU for scrypt. On a
memory-constrained host that is also an unauthenticated resource-amplification
lever. README already assigns login rate-limiting to the reverse proxy, so that
part stays the operator's job — but the timing oracle is fixable here.

## Fix

In auth.login(), when no account row matches, still perform a
check_password_hash against a fixed dummy hash (generated once at import time)
before raising invalid_credentials, so both paths do the same scrypt work.

Then either keep the README claim (now true) or, if the equalisation is judged
imperfect, soften it the way the neighbouring "Known, accepted trade-off"
section handles registration enumeration.

## Verification

Test asserting the two paths' timings are within a small factor of each other
(a ratio assertion, not an absolute one — absolute timings vary by host).
title: login: timing side channel enumerates accounts, contradicting the README's no-enumeration claim
